articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 23, 2026. This action targets entities and individuals deemed to be involved in activities supporting the Iranian regime.

These designations are part of ongoing efforts to exert pressure on Iran and disrupt its illicit networks. The specifics of the designated parties and the nature of their activities were detailed in the official announcement.
This move follows a series of similar actions taken by OFAC against Iran in recent weeks, underscoring a continued focus on restricting the country's access to the international financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designations and Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to Iran on November 20, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC also issued updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning Cuba sanctions.

The Iran designations aim to further restrict the financial activities of individuals and entities supporting the Iranian government. The Cuba FAQs provide additional guidance and clarification for navigating the existing sanctions regime against Cuba.
These actions reflect OFAC's dual focus on addressing ongoing concerns regarding Iran's activities and providing clarity for compliance with Cuba-related regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Counter Narcotics and Cyber Actors, Amends Russia GL
body: On November 19, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to combating these threats globally.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License to facilitate certain transactions, and an amended Russia-related General License along with updated Frequently Asked Questions. These updates aim to refine existing sanctions programs and provide necessary guidance for compliance.

The amended Russia-related General License and FAQs reflect ongoing adjustments to the sanctions regime in response to evolving geopolitical circumstances, particularly concerning the conflict in Ukraine.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist organizations and activities.

This action is part of a broader strategy to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist groups and prevent them from accessing resources. The U.S. government continues to prioritize efforts to counter global terrorism.
The specific details of the designated parties and the nature of their involvement in terrorism were outlined in OFAC's official release, reinforcing the commitment to safeguarding national security.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism
body: On November 13, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This dual focus highlights the interconnectedness of these illicit networks.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of organizations engaged in drug trafficking and supporting terrorist acts. The U.S. government continues to employ sanctions as a tool to combat these threats.
The action reinforces the commitment to international security and the protection of the U.S. financial system from exploitation by criminal and terrorist organizations.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Information
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an update to existing Iran designations on November 9, 2026. This update provides additional information or modifications to previously announced sanctions.

Such updates are routine and ensure the accuracy and effectiveness of the sanctions list. They may include changes to identifying information or other details related to designated individuals or entities.
The continuous refinement of sanctions data is crucial for maintaining compliance and ensuring that the measures remain targeted and impactful against the Iranian regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Iran-Related Designations
body: On November 6, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations. These actions target additional individuals and entities supporting the Iranian government's destabilizing activities.

The designations aim to further isolate Iran from the international financial system and curtail its ability to fund illicit programs. This is part of a sustained campaign of pressure against the regime.
The U.S. government continues to monitor and respond to Iran's actions, utilizing sanctions as a key tool to promote regional and global security.

body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related actors and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt malicious cyber activities and international criminal networks.

Additionally, OFAC issued new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination. These measures reinforce the existing sanctions regime against Cuba and address specific concerns related to the country's activities.
The designations highlight the U.S. government's commitment to combating a wide range of illicit activities that pose threats to national security and the global financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Iran Designations, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: On November 4, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and provided updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's destabilizing behavior.

In addition to the Iran-focused measures, OFAC published an Iran-related alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License along with a Frequently Asked Question. The Venezuela update aims to provide clarity and adjust specific aspects of the sanctions program.
These comprehensive actions demonstrate OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, addressing both new threats and refining existing measures to ensure effectiveness and compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are often issued to clarify the scope of sanctions programs or to permit specific activities that would otherwise be prohibited. This particular amendment aims to facilitate certain humanitarian or other authorized transactions.
The issuance of amended General Licenses is a regular practice by OFAC to ensure that sanctions programs are implemented effectively while minimizing unintended consequences.

articles.headline: UK Imposes Sanctions Under Global Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law Regime
body: On November 24, 2026, the UK government imposed sanctions under the Global Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law Sanctions Regulations 2026. This marks the first set of designations under this new sanctions regime.

One individual, Mohamed MOUFLEH, was designated and is now subject to an asset freeze, travel ban, and director disqualification sanction. The Secretary of State cited reasonable grounds to suspect MOUFLEH as an involved person under the regulations.
This new regime allows the UK to target individuals and entities responsible for serious human rights violations and abuses, as well as breaches of international humanitarian law, globally.

articles.headline: OFSI Issues Sanctions Notice for Russia, Specifies LNG Tanker
body: On November 20, 2026, the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) issued a sanctions notice under The Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. This notice specified the LNG tanker 'LNG SOARS' (IMO 9307205) under shipping sanctions.

The Secretary of State has reasonable grounds to suspect that LNG SOARS is an involved entity due to its likely involvement in activities destabilizing Ukraine or undermining its territorial integrity, sovereignty, or independence. Specifically, the vessel is suspected of carrying goods from Russia to a third country that could contribute to these actions.
As a result, the specified ship is prohibited from accessing UK ports, may have its UK Ship Register registration terminated, and its master or pilot may face port barring or detention directions.

articles.headline: BIS Adds Seven Entities in Southeast Asia to Entity List
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a final rule on November 23, 2026, amending the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to add seven entities to the Entity List.

These entities, located in Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand, were added due to a significant risk that they are or could become involved in diverting advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users. The additions include MSFusion Sdn. Bhd., PT Megaspeed International, and Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd in Malaysia; Apex Enterprise Solutions (Singapore) Private Limited, Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd, and Swiftdata (Pte.) Ltd. in Singapore; and Megaspeed (Thailand) Co., Ltd. in Thailand.

For each listed entity, a license is now required for all items subject to the EAR, and license applications will be subject to a presumption of denial. A savings clause allows certain shipments already en route on November 23, 2026, to proceed under previous eligibility, provided the export, reexport, or transfer is completed by December 23, 2026.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
